reader.summary: The defining event of the week was Chile's president making the first state visit to Bolivia in 71 years, a landmark diplomatic reset driven by both countries' shift to right-wing governments. During the visit, Bolivia formally set aside its decades-old maritime claim against Chile, opening what commentators called a new era of bilateral cooperation. In domestic finance, Chilean pension funds (AFP) came under sharp criticism after heavy losses on interest-rate derivative bets. Lawmakers accused fund managers of amplifying risk while internal warnings about exposure had been raised in advance, sparking calls for tighter oversight of derivative trading. The copper sector saw two simultaneous de-escalations: Antofagasta workers agreed to end their strike, and supervisors at BHP's Escondida mine reached a deal to avert a walkout. Meanwhile, an Austrian investor moved quickly to boost output at an older Chilean mine. Unusually wet and snowy spring conditions brought an avalanche that killed three climbers, fresh mudslides in the central valleys, and a ski resort that extended its season. Smaller stories included a Venezuelan gang member receiving a 20-year sentence for kidnapping and killing a Chilean dissident, and Isabel Allende winning Spain's Planeta literary prize. The previous week's 2027 budget proposal, Centinela mine dispute, constitutional security bill, and Zaliasnik controversy produced no new headlines this window.

display.eli5:
Chile and Bolivia just had their first big diplomatic meeting in over 70 years. Both countries now have right-wing governments, so they are teaming up on trade and borders. Next week, expect to see actual signed agreements, not just handshakes and speeches. This is the biggest story, called the Chile-Bolivia diplomatic follow-up.

On the money side, Chile's pension funds lost a lot of money on risky bets about interest rates. The managers were warned beforehand but ignored the warnings. Next week, lawmakers will push a new rule to limit how much risk those funds can take. Think of it like a parent telling a teenager they cannot spend all their allowance on one fancy gadget. This is the pension fund derivative oversight story.

In the mining world, two big copper strikes just ended. That is good for the economy. An investor from Austria is also moving fast to get an older mine producing again. The copper story will get quieter next week as things settle down.

A surprise would be if the left-wing politicians in Chile's parliament get angry about how easily Bolivia dropped its old claim to the sea, and they demand a big public debate about it. That would be a political fight nobody saw coming right after the handshakes.
